title: The wooden board
hookLine: a wooden board struck to call the monks, often inscribed: life and death are grave, time passes swiftly

cards: Clack. Then faster and faster, a wooden rattle rolling across the courtyard until it runs out, and stops. Outside a Zen hall there often hangs a thick, heavy board of wood, and someone stands before it with a mallet.
The sound tells everyone: come to sit. Walk up close and you may see words brushed on its face. Their message, in plain English: life and death are a great matter.

teach.h: A PLANK OF WOOD, A MALLET.
teach.b: First, what it is. In Japanese it's called the han: a plank of hard wood hung by cords, struck with a wooden mallet. It calls the community to zazen, and in some places marks the start of the day's sittings.
Its sound isn't musical like a bell. It's dry and blunt, more a knock on the door than a song. Second, the words.

teach.h: WORDS: LIFE AND DEATH ARE GREAT.
teach.b: The inscription varies, but the common message, in paraphrase, runs like this: the matter of life and death is great; everything passes, and passes quickly; wake up; don't waste this time. It's not decoration.
It's the reason for the sitting, written on the thing that calls you to sit.
Third, the board wears through. Struck day after day, the wood slowly wears down, and some boards end up with a hollow, or a hole right through the center where the mallet lands.
The board teaches impermanence by being used up. Every strike that calls the monks takes a little of the board away.
Time passes swiftly is not a threat. It's a reminder, said plainly, the way a friend might tap your shoulder. In Zen, remembering that life is short isn't meant to make people anxious.
It's meant to wake them up to this hour, this breath, this conversation, while it's here. The board doesn't say hurry. It says notice, because this won't come again.

how: In Zen monasteries and centers a wooden board called the han hangs outside the meditation hall and is struck in a set rhythm to call people to sit; it often carries an inscription about the urgency of life and death and the swift passing of time.

games.q: you read the board: time passes swiftly, don't waste this life. what is it asking you to do?
o: wake up to this hour while it's here.
games.why: the message is a reminder, not a whip: notice this moment, because it won't come again. then go and sit.

practice: Tap something gently, a table, a book, your own knee, and listen until the sound is completely gone. Tap again, letting each one be a small han, a call back to this moment, and notice that the last sound has already passed.
After a few, stop tapping and simply sit, listening.

wordCard.voice: The wooden board. The han, struck to call a Zen community to sit, and often inscribed with a reminder: life and death are a great matter, time passes swiftly. Today's word.
